query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing Ta with Nb in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce the overall density without sacrificing its high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr, with a density of 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Elemental substitution: Replace Ta with Nb to produce an as‐cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under tensile/compressive loads at room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C, using standard as‐cast processing protocols without additional heat treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC (solid solution) microstructure, maintained primarily by lattice distortion and solid–solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Nb, being lighter (density ≈8.57 g/cm³) than Ta (density ≈16.65 g/cm³) but having similar refractory properties and atomic size, is expected to lower the alloy’s density while preserving the solid–solution strengthening and phase stability that contribute to high strength. The substitution should minimally perturb the electronic structure and lattice distortion, thereby retaining the alloy’s high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ with retention of high yield and tensile strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g/cm³ and known high-temperature strength.
generation.boundary: The alloy is assessed under mechanical loading conditions typical of high–temperature structural applications, specifically from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the density reduction and any subtle effects on phase stability and high–temperature strength remain to be quantified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the as‐cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy by substituting Ta with an equivalent atomic percentage of Nb, using identical casting conditions as for HfMoTaTiZr. Conduct density measurements using Archimedes’ method, and perform standardized tensile/compressive tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C. Additionally, use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to verify the phase structure and microstructural integrity.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C
Microstructural evaluation (phase identification via XRD, morphology via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not show a significant decrease in density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ or if the measured mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, ductility) at room temperature and high temperature (≈1000 °C) fall below acceptable thresholds when compared to the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. chosen.lever: elemental substitution (replacing Hf with the lighter Nb)
chosen.technique: Arc-melting synthesis followed by homogenization heat treatment and subsequent tensile/compressive testing
chosen.conditions: Measurements performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C) under controlled loading conditions
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by reducing the alloy’s density via a controlled compositional change. By partially substituting Hf with Nb—a lighter refractory element with an adequate melting point—one can achieve a lower density while preserving the high-temperature mechanical strength. The approach utilizes standard synthesis techniques (arc melting and heat treatment) and established high-temperature mechanical tests, aligning well with prior evidence in high-entropy alloy design and offering a clear falsification test: if the mechanical performance at ~1000 °C falls below that of the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the intervention would be rejected.

frame.system: An as‐cast refractory high‐entropy alloy with nominal composition HfMoTaTiZr, where the alloy’s current state exhibits high strength at room and elevated temperatures (up to ~1000 °C) but has a relatively high density of 10.21 g/cm³.
frame.goal: Reduce the alloy's density while maintaining its high mechanical strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (ca. 1000 °C).
frame.limitation: The high overall density, driven by the inclusion of intrinsically heavy elements, potentially limiting applications where weight is critical.
root_cause_cues: without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C
constraints: The intervention must be a single change to the alloy system (i.e. a single compositional or processing adjustment)
Mechanical properties (strength at room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C) must not be sacrificed
The alloy should remain in the as‐cast state without relying on post‐casting heat–treatments or complex processing modifications
frame.regime: Mechanical loading conditions relevant to high–temperature structural applications; tests should cover room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C.
prior_attempts: Literature on high–entropy or refractory alloys using substitutions to reduce density has shown that minor compositional modifications (e.g. replacing one heavy element with a lighter, yet similarly refractory, element) can lower density, but many substitutions can adversely affect phase stability or high–temperature strength.
frame.intervention_proposal: Substitute the element tantalum (Ta) with niobium (Nb) in the alloy formulation. Nb is a lighter refractory metal (density ≈8.57 g cm⁻³ compared to Ta’s ≈16.65 g cm⁻³) with similar atomic radius and comparable high–temperature strength, which should help lower the overall density without compromising the mechanical properties.
frame.mechanism: The mechanism is based on a targeted compositional tuning: by replacing the heaviest constituent (Ta) with a lighter element (Nb) that still retains the requisite strength and high–temperature stability, the alloy’s overall density is reduced. Nb's similar electronic structure and crystal chemistry ensure the phase stability and alloy strengthening mechanisms (such as lattice distortion and solid–solution strengthening) remain largely preserved.

predicted_directional_changes.density: Decrease relative to the as–cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy
predicted_directional_changes.mechanical_properties: Retention of high yield and tensile strength at room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C

frame.applicable_temperature_and_loading_bound: The performance must be maintained at room temperature and under tensile/compressive loads sustained at temperatures up to ca. 1000 °C, typical of refractory and high–temperature structural applications.
frame.supporting_prior_evidence: Prior studies in refractory high–entropy alloys have demonstrated that substituting heavy elements with lighter ones (for instance, Nb replacing Ta) can reduce density while preserving or even enhancing high–temperature strength and phase stability. Similar substitution strategies have been reported in the literature, highlighting Nb’s comparable mechanical behavior in high–temperature regimes.
frame.proposed_experiment: Synthesize an as–cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy (i.e. substitute Ta with Nb) using identical casting methods as for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize its physical density via Archimedes’ method and evaluate its mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C) using standardized tensile testing. Microstructural analysis (using XRD and SEM) should be conducted to verify phase stability and confirm the formation of the desired solid–solution phase.
frame.rejection_criterion: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a significant reduction in density (targeting a decrease from 10.21 g cm⁻³ by a quantifiable margin) or if the high–temperature (≈1000 °C) mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength) fall below an acceptable threshold compared to the as–cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline (for example, a decrease beyond an industry–acceptable margin), the hypothesis of a successful substitution would be falsified.

decision.trend: Over the past several years, researchers in refractory high‐entropy alloys have increasingly used compositional tuning—especially elemental substitution—to optimize the tradeoff between high strength and reduced density. Early work established that as‐cast HEAs can achieve high strength and ductility, while later studies showed that even one‐atom substitutions (e.g. replacing one heavy refractory component with a lighter yet similarly refractory element) can reduce density without sacrificing high‐temperature performance. However, most prior attempts involved alloys containing both Ta and Nb, or required additional processing steps to stabilize the desired phases.
decision.unsolved: No study to date has directly demonstrated in the as‐cast state that a single, targeted substitution (specifically replacing the heavy Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr) will reduce density while maintaining mechanical properties up to approximately 1000 °C. How this substitution affects phase stability and solid solution strengthening under minimal processing remains to be verified.
decision.lever: elemental substitution of Ta with Nb
decision.why: This step follows the established trend of using lighter refractory elements to reduce overall density while retaining high-temperature strength. Previous studies (e.g., PMC5578249) have shown that Nb can match Ta’s performance in refractory HEAs. Given that the as‐cast condition is mandated, substituting Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr is the most plausible next step, as it directly addresses the density limitation and leverages Nb’s similar atomic properties and solid solution strengthening mechanisms.
